stories.title: Nvidia has no obvious successor to Jensen Huang — and that's a problem
stories.summary: Nvidia is coming under fire for having no clear succession plan to replace Jensen Huang in the event that something unexpected happens — like an international incident with him at the center . Why it matters: The spotlight on Huang shows the vulnerabilities of a large company being dependent on one executive — and the risks it poses to investors and customers, corporate governance experts tell...

sources.title: Schumer accuses Trump of defending Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at cost of national security
sources.text: Democratic leader Sen. Charles Schumer ripped President Donald Trump on Tuesday for defending embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the expense of U.S. national security. "The press reports that Trump was briefed more than a year ago that Nvidia's CEO was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and Trump didn't do anything – anything – about it," Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the Senate floor. "Can you believe that?" said Schumer, the Senate's minority leader. Schumer's broadside came on the heels of New York Times reports that Trump had been briefed about Huang's extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — whom U.S. intelligence concluded was a spy for China — and opted not to do anything about it. Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he only recently learned of the allegations about Alice Huang, and the president commented Monday that he "really" believes Jensen Huang's claim to him directly that he had no idea Alice Huang was a spy. "One of our most important companies that is involved in national security, and the CEO might be having an affair with a Chinese spy, and Trump did nothing about it," Schumer said Tuesday. "What a dereliction of duty. He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends," Schumer said. "Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security. It's that simple, it's obvious." Schumer's comments escalated growing bipartisan concern in Congress about the Nvidia CEO and his company. Nvidia makes advanced chips that are essential components in developing artificial intelligence models, a sector that is the focus of keen competition between the United States and China. Schumer noted that Trump earlier this year invited Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing, and that he took Huang's advice by granting the People's Republic of China "access to some of our most advanced AI chips." Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump's controversial White House ballroom project, the Democrat said. "Despite talking a big game, Trump continues to show a troubling resistance to confront China on AI and to protect American national security," Schumer said. "I've been saying it for years: our cutting-edge AI chips are too valuable to fall into the hands of potential adversaries." Schumer in his speech called on Republicans to join Democrats in passing several pieces of legislation — the AI Overwatch Act, the Match Act, and the Chip Security Act — which he said would "cut off China's access to advanced American technology." "We also need answers on Nvidia's influence campaign and how [it] affected the Trump administration's national security decisions, including the loosening – the loosening – of key export controls," Schumer said. "We need a full accounting for Trump's failure to address foreign espionage in the American tech industry." CNBC has requested comment from the White House about Schumer's remarks. The remarks came nearly a week after Democrats won enough Senate and House races nationwide to take majority control of both chambers of Congress in January. Schumer hopes to be selected majority leader. Regardless of which Democrats are tapped to serve as majority leaders in both chambers, the party will have the ability to launch investigations into Nvidia and Huang. Earlier Tuesday, Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., said on CNBC's " Squawk Box " that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang. Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips. And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang. "If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said. "We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible." Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday, a day after Nvidia announced it was opening an independent investigation into Jensen Huang's conduct. Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, raised concerns that the scandal could plague talks over export controls for advanced AI chips. "It's important not to have a personal scandal interfere with the substantive policy discussion about to what degree we should be allowing the export of cutting edge chips to our geopolitical competitors like China," Obernolte told CNBC. "I hope this isn't a distraction because that's a very important conversation that needs to happen." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , D-N.Y., said at a news conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security." Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote. sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy: a timeline
sources.text: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote . “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. sources.title: NVIDIA shareholders are suing the company and CEO Jensen Huang
sources.text: The company’s shares have plummeted in response to the exec’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The unfolding drama around NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman now accused of being a spy for the Chinese government may be getting its first courtroom chapter. A shareholder in the computing giant has sued accusing NVIDIA and Huang of misleading investors about the nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Taiwanese company Megaspeed who is now suspected of being an espionage asset for China. Huang is a common surname; The pair are not related. Mark Kistenmacher filed the complaint and is seeking class action status for anyone who purchased NVIDIA shares between October 9 and November 8. The first date is when The New York Times published a story on NVIDIA and Megaspeed detailing a connection between the pair, which was rebuffed by NVIDIA as a routine business relationship; the second date is when the NVIDIA founder admitted to an affair and the company publicly disclosed that it was launching its own investigation into whether its top exec had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. In the interim, The New York Times published an in-depth feature on October 29 claiming that the NVIDIA CEO had become the subject of a suspected Chinese intelligence action. The piece cites NVIDIA representative John Rizzo, who said, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." This statement, the lawsuit alleges, was not true. The company's shares have dropped in the fallout of the allegations, with NVIDIA on track to lose more than $470 billion in market value over the past two days. "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint states.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
sources.text: Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large. He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares. But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair. Initially , Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang , an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader. Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.” Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication. In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children. “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.” Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton. Spencer , for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan. In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.” Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board. “The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.” Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said. “Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.” Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate. Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly. Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value. “When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said

sources.title: Nvidia board member Stephen Neal could play big role in probe of CEO Jensen Huang
sources.text: Nvidia's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy may hinge on decisions by company board member Stephen Neal , a longtime white-collar defense attorney whose extensive resume includes dealing with corporate scandals. Neal, the former CEO of the Cooley law firm, is Nvidia's lead independent director and head of corporate governance. Nvidia has not named the investigators who will probe the allegations surrounding Huang, but the company has said its board is leading the probe with help from outside counsel. Neal's experience makes him a likely key figure in the investigation. Nvidia's board has said there is "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" by Huang's admitted affair with Alice Huang, who had been an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer. China dismissed U.S. intelligence conclusions that Alice Huang was a spy, which were first reported by The New York Times . Jensen Huang, one of the most powerful businessmen in the artificial intelligence boom, has said he would "cooperate fully" with the investigation. Nvidia's board has 10 independent members, including a former president of Taco Bell , a former Eli Lilly executive, and a former vice chairman from Goldman Sachs . Neal has litigated cases across securities, bankruptcies, antitrust, takeovers and more, according to his Cooley bio. And he's conducted several investigations for multiple boards of directors, including at General Motors , where he advised the company in disputes with Ross Perot. Neal has also conducted several investigations for committees of directors and independent directors, though most of those client names are confidential. He's also handled investigations with the Securities and Exchange Commission for both corporations and individuals. When he joined Nvidia, Neal was also the chairman of the board of directors at Levi Strauss . He stepped down in 2021 after reaching the mandatory board retirement age of 72, the company said at the time. The retailer did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Monday. Neal joined Nvidia's board in 2019. He is chairman emeritus and senior counsel at Cooley, and was the firm's CEO from 2001 to 2008. Neal did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Neal's past clients include Elizabeth Holmes , the convicted fraudster who founded the blood-testing startup Theranos, and late financier Charles Keating Jr . Neal and other Cooley lawyers represented Holmes in a class-action civil lawsuit in Arizona federal court over Theranos' blood-testing services, which produced bogus results. In September 2019, Neal and his colleagues asked to be removed from the case because Holmes could not pay their legal bills. A judge granted that withdrawal motion less than two months later. In 1989, Neal was hired to represent Keating, who had become the face of the massive savings and loan scandal in the United States as head of American Continental, which owned the California-based thrift Lincoln Savings & Loan. Keating's campaign contributions to five U.S. senators — none of whom were charged with wrongdoing — earned them the notorious sobriquet "The Keating Five." Keating was sentenced in 1992 to up to 10 years in prison by Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Lance Ito for an extensive fraud. Ito later gained fame as the judge in O.J. Simpson's murder trial. Keating ended up serving less than five years after that conviction and a federal one were overturned on appeal. Neal represented Keating in his efforts to overturn his convictions. In a 1997 article about Keating, Time magazine called Neal "the legal Houdini behind his release." Neal also has ties in and around Silicon Valley. In November 2022, in the wake of the collapse of the $32 billion cryptocurrency firm FTX, the company's founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, nominated Neal to serve as chairman of the board of FTX Trading, the FTX-affiliated hedge fund Alameda Research, and a third affiliate, West Realm Shires, as part of a Chapter 11 bankruptcy petition. But Cooley said Neal was "unable to serve in" those positions, Business Insider reported at the time. Neal received his law degree from Stanford, where Bankman-Fried's parents had been law professors. Neal is also chairperson of the trust for Meta's Oversight Board , which is responsible for examining whether Meta's decisions to remove or leave up content on Facebook, Instagram or Threads were in line with the company's policies and values. And on Tuesday, the journalist Theo Baker, whose articles as a freshman reporter on The Stanford Daily at Stanford University about allegations against that school's president Marc Tessier-Lavinge led to his resignation, said in an X post that Tessier-Lavinge had hired Neal "to try to stop my reporting on allegations of research misconduct from coming out." Cooley's history with Nvidia goes back decades. The law firm said it incorporated the company in 1993 and has served as its principal outside corporate and litigation counsel for roughly three decades. Cooley handled Nvidia's initial public offering in 1999. Investors will be closely watching the investigation, and its emphasis on independence, as the process unfolds, according to Brayden King, a professor of management and organizations at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management. "You definitely want somebody leading it who people can look at and say, 'OK, we believe this is a report that we can fully believe and trust that the outcome is the right outcome,'" King said. "That's what investors are looking for. They just don't like the instability that comes with all of this." King said the Nvidia investigation sits at a unique intersection of Wall Street and Washington, where the company is likely navigating its next steps to try to appease both groups. sources.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
sources.text: Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says. Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions. Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says. Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.” But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. sources.title: Claude can now join your weekly meeting to take notes and even start work for you — and that's not all, with new spreadsheet, whiteboard tools and more helping conquer the world of "Frontier Work"
sources.text: Anthropic wants Claude to help with "work at the frontier" Anthropic has unveiled a host of updates for Claude which could see the AI platform play a much more integral role in some of your most common work tasks. Among the next expansions are tools which allow Claude to join video calls as a participant, meaning it learns first-hand from your meetings and can start work immediately. Joining its existing suite of office software tools are new Whiteboards, Sheets and Data services looking to help users work and create more effectively - and new interactive connectors will now allow Claude to work inside the full versions of common workplace apps such as Adobe , Atlassian and HubSpot. "A year ago, Claude changed how developers work," Anthropic wrote in a blog post announcing the new tools. "Engineers stopped asking AI for snippets and started handing it whole tasks, which freed them to spend their time deciding what to build. For most other teams, work has stayed much the same: the email gets written a little faster, the meeting comes with a summary." "Now the frontier is moving to knowledge work, and people are starting to hand Claude whole tasks too." The most striking new addition is undoubtedly Claude Meetings, which will allow Claude to join video calls as a visible participant. Claude follows the conversation and starts on the work as people talk, taking notes, drafting plans, outlining timelines on whiteboards, answering chat questions, and utilizing connected work apps while conversations happen - and when the call ends, the notes, action items and everything Claude made are waiting in claude.ai. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Also new is Claude Whiteboards, a shared, real-time board which helps teams turn brainstorms and retrospectives into structured plans, timelines, and action items, and integrates directly into Claude Meetings, and Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet tool which allows teams to build and edit trackers and budgets collaboratively with Claude, complete with tabs, formulas, and dropdown menus. Finally, Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards) connects company data sources (such as CRMs and warehouses) to generate dashboards, data stories, and narrated videos, featuring beta capabilities like certified queries and live sharing. Alongside this, new Interactive Connectors will allow full versions of partner tools (like Adobe, Atlassian, HubSpot, Salesforce , NetSuite, and Workday) to open directly inside Claude, which can take actions directly within these apps with user approval.
